plays_group.name: Convene
plays_group.teaser: Bring together a diverse cross-section of your community, organize them around a shared vision, and keep them engaged with ongoing opportunities to grow professionally and participate in the creation of a community of practice.

question.question_details: What are your overall goals for convening your network?
What is the call to action for convening? Why should people want to convene at all? What will the network offer people that they do not currently have?
What challenge or opportunity will bring people together? Does your community have a particular specialty or focus area to rally people around?
Are you seeking to formalize a body of professionals already working together informally? Expanding participation by bringing new people into the network? Starting from scratch?
How will your convening strategies generate opportunities for cross-sector collaboration among the potential network partners you’ve already identified?
Who will take the overall lead in convening your network?

play.name: Small Groups
play.excerpt: Host open and informal meetings for small groups of network members with shared interests to provide ongoing opportunities for network members to meet, share, and collaborate, whether in face-to-face meetups or through online webinars and hangouts.

advice.advice_details: Decide what you will bring people together to speak about—the formation of the network itself or a particular approach to learning that the network can implement.

advice.advice_heading: Pick a date, time, and location
advice.advice_details: Get the basics of an invitation together by choosing a date 4-6 weeks in the future and securing a meeting space. Even a café or diner can work as a starting point. Also think about how frequent these convenings should be.

Identify people you want to bring together, being mindful of their interests, availability, and potential contribution to the network. To start, aim for 10-16 invitees, anticipating 8-12 actual attendees.
Include a general outline of the meeting agenda with your invitation and encourage participants to add their own discussion items or come with materials to share.
Ask for a group member to serve as temporary secretary, taking meeting notes and keeping track of what group members are asked to do and what commitments they make.
Following the meeting, revise and publish your notes, along with any images (drawn or photographed) that illustrate what the group talked about and sharing any specific calls-to-action.

example.name: Meet-ups
example.description: Educators and community members interested in maker learning meet regularly to tour different makerspaces in Pittsburgh, share ideas, and try new techniques, test out new fabrication equipment, and make plans for maker learning projects.

example.name: Affinity Groups
example.description: Early childhood educators, specialists, and researchers representing both front-line education centers and service agencies, as well as advocacy organizations and research institutions, gather to review current challenges, digest recent research, and work toward a shared agenda for Pittsburgh’s youngest learners.

example.name: Webinars & Hangouts
example.description: Administrators from Elizabeth Forward School District partner with ed-tech firm Zulama Learning to host monthly Google+ Hangouts on game-based learning, helping to create a community of educators and game designers ready to collaborate.

example.name: Role-based Roundtables
example.description: The Sprout Fund hosts a quarterly Communications Roundtable for network members who work in marketing, promotions, and public relations at different organizations so that communications professionals can keep each other informed.

play.name: Lunch & Learns
play.excerpt: Create opportunities for network members to share their expertise and demonstrate their work for other network members by hosting daytime lunch-and-learn events or evening happy hour gatherings where attendees can learn from one another and consider how they may take advantage of ideas, practices, and upcoming opportunities.

advice.advice_heading: Set your goals for the event
advice.advice_details: Identify your audience and determine what you want them to learn and/or do as a result of participating in the event. This will guide the rest of your decisions. Keep the goals few and simple.

Identify someone from your network or a visitor to your community who has an interesting perspective on learning, a new project or product they’d like to present on, or a conversation they’d like to start.

advice.advice_heading: Pick a date, time, and location
advice.advice_details: Get the basics of an invitation together by choosing a date 4-6 weeks in the future and securing a meeting space.
Simple boxed lunches, a selection of wraps, or a build-your-own burrito spread are all affordable options to feed a small group.

Get the word out through your newsletter and social media accounts. Ask the venue to add the event to their calendar, and provide the speaker with content to share with his or her professional contacts.
Ask the presenter to share a general outline of their presentation in advance and develop some discussion questions you can have ready for the Q & A portion of the lunch and learn.
Create a record of the event that you can share with network members who aren’t able to make it. If the event is the first of its kind, consider inviting the press as well.

example.name: Conference Report-Outs
example.description: After a delegation of Pittsburghers returned from the annual Digital Media & Learning conference, they reported on their experience and noted opportunities for the Remake Learning Network at a DML Lunch & Learn.

example.name: Topic of Interest
example.description: Given the growing interest in 3D printing among both makers and educators, the creators of the Additive Project shared examples of their flexible, open-sourced, project-based curricula for using 3D printing both in school and out-of-school.

example.name: Upcoming Opportunity
example.description: When The Sprout Fund launched a new funding stream to support Connected Learning projects through its Hive program, Sprout funding programs staffers hosted a Lunch & Learn to help community members develop a functional understanding of Connected Learning.

example.name: Network Luminary
example.description: In support of his book Robot Futures, CREATE Lab director Illah Nourbakhsh presented an exploration of the social challenges created by new technologies and opportunities for Remake Learning to create learning opportunities that meet these pressing challenges.

play.name: Professional Development
play.excerpt: Offer professional development sessions and continuing education credits to educators and other professionals seeking to incorporate new and innovative teaching methods into their practice, or partner with established professional development agencies to offer credit at network events and activities so that more educators find valuable professional opportunities at network events.

advice.advice_details: Identify a school or support agency in your community who can provide continuing education credits and reach out to them to begin planning.
Work with an innovative educator in your network to develop a workshop session that turns their innovative approach into a training session, or search for such resources on the web.
Share information about the session with school administrators and others who can contact educators directly and invite them to participate.
If possible, dedicate a small amount of follow-on funding to support educators interested in putting their new knowledge into practice through a pilot project.
Work with professional development providers to turn the session into a resource kit you can make available to even more educators.

Gather external resources or prepare your own materials for educators to use as an ongoing reference. Keep in touch with educators after they leave the session and support their progress as they implement ideas in their classroom.

example.name: Network Innovators as PD Providers
example.description: The Children’s Innovation Project partner with national PD provider ASSET STEM Education to adapt innovative lessons developed in the classroom into models for interdisciplinary learning other teachers can use.

example.name: Interest-based PD
example.description: The Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh hosts a Maker Educator Boot Camp, a free professional development workshop for K-12 teachers interested in bringing maker practices into their classrooms.

example.name: Physical Space
example.description: The Allegheny Intermediate Unit created transformED as a "digital playground" where teachers can work together to develop classroom applications for tech tools like Hummingbird Robotics Kits, e-textiles, 3D printers, and more.

example.name: Offer Credits at Network Events
example.description: The Sprout Fund partnered with PAEYC, an agency that can issue professional development credits, to offer credits to educators participating in the Pittsburgh Learning Pathways Summit, making the event even more worthwhile to teachers.

play.name: Network Engagement Events
play.excerpt: Invite all network members to gather for important occasional events where members can establish relationships, focus their attention on issues and opportunities of critical importance, collaborate directly in facilitated discussions, reflect on past accomplishments and look ahead to potential future opportunities.

advice.advice_heading: Set your goals for the event
advice.advice_details: Identify your audience and determine what you want them to learn and/or do as a result of participating in the event. This will guide the rest of your decisions. Keep the goals few and simple.

advice.advice_heading: Pick a date, time, and location
advice.advice_details: Get the basics of an invitation together by choosing a date 12-16 weeks in the future and securing a meeting space.

advice.advice_heading: Plan the program & build a budget
advice.advice_details: Decide the format of your event, sketch out a floor plan, draft a basic agenda, and create a run-of-show. Tabulate your anticipated expenses for the venue rental, food and refreshments, event logistics, and any speaker or programming costs.
Once you’ve confirmed the basics, send a save the date no more than 10 weeks in advance. Send a real invitation with registration details at least 6 weeks prior to the event.

Use discussion techniques like human-centered design to engage event participants in productive conversations. Start with a topic, theme, or challenge, and guide them through collaborative activities that generate new ideas.
Create a record of the event that you can share with network members who aren’t able to make it. If the event is the first of its kind, consider inviting the press as well.

example.name: Making Sparks
example.description: To generate new ideas for innovative learning projects, The Sprout Fund hosted Making Sparks, an event that facilitated collaborative brainstorming among educators and innovators, and tied real funding resources to the outcome.

example.name: Pittsburgh Learning Pathways Summit
example.description: The Pittsburgh Learning Pathways Summit brought together educators and students from more than 30 regional school districts to take a leading role in the ongoing development of digital badges for learning through the Remake Learning Network.

example.name: CONTEXT
example.description: The CREATE Lab at Carnegie Mellon hosted CONTEXT, a conference focusing on how educators implement technology in practical ways in their classrooms and out-of-school learning environments.

example.name: Network Primer
example.description: Shortly after the Remake Learning Network first formalized, Carnegie Mellon University hosted a day-long event that threw the doors open to the previously small and informal network, attracting more than 500 educators and innovators.

play.name: Annual Conferences
play.excerpt: Host or partner on annual events for specific groups of network members such as education technology conferences for entrepreneurs and commercial partners, academic summits for researchers and scholars, and professional development events for out-of-school educators or early childhood education specialists.

advice.advice_heading: Set your goals for the event
advice.advice_details: Identify your audience and determine what you want them to learn and/or do as a result of participating in the event. This will guide the rest of your decisions. Keep the goals few and simple.

advice.advice_heading: Pick a date, time, and location
advice.advice_details: Get the basics of an invitation together by choosing a date at least six months in the future and securing a meeting space.
Identify speakers and exhibitors, invite them to participate, and find out their technical, space, and media needs.

advice.advice_heading: Plan the program & build a budget
advice.advice_details: Decide the format of your event, sketch out a floor plan, draft a basic agenda, and create a run-of-show. Tabulate your anticipated expenses for the venue rental, food and refreshments, event logistics, and any speaker or programming costs.
Once you’ve confirmed the basics, send a save the date no more than 16 weeks in advance. Send a real invitation with registration details at least 12 weeks prior to the event.
Create a record of the event that you can share with network members who aren’t able to make it. If the event is the first of its kind, consider inviting the press as well.

example.name: TRETC
example.description: The Pittsburgh Technology Council hosts the Three Rivers Education Technology Conference to connect ed-tech entrepreneurs and enterprise-scale with administrators and educators from regional school districts to scope out the latest in ed-tech gear.

example.name: FredForward
example.description: The Fred Rogers Center for Early Learning and Children’s Media invites thought leaders, researchers, and producers of children’s media from all over the world to visit Pittsburgh for an agenda-setting conference at the intersection of education and entertainment.

example.name: PAEYC Conference & UnConference
example.description: The Pittsburgh Association for the Education of Young Children hosts an alternating Conference & UnConfernece event each year, giving Pittsburgh-area early childhood educators an opportunity to hear from national leaders at the conference, while working together as peers at the UnConference.

example.name: CREate Festival
example.description: Celebrating the intersection of creativity and technology, the CREate Festival is part showcase, part trade show, and part innovation summit with an entire track of programming dedicated to highlight innovations led by the Remake Learning Network.

play.name: External Speakers
play.excerpt: Invite thought leaders to visit your community and speak to network members as a means of importing knowledge and creating opportunities for partnership and collaboration with other regions also working to remake learning.

advice.advice_heading: Set your goals for the event
advice.advice_details: Identify your audience and determine what you want them to learn and how they will use this new knowledge in their practice. This will guide the rest of your decisions. Keep the goals few and simple.

Survey the national landscape of writers, speakers, and leaders you pay attention to and can get in touch with. Find the speaker’s appropriate contact, which might be a speakers’ bureau or manager, and reach out with a formal invitation to speak to your network.

Based on the dates of your speaker’s availability and intended audience, rent or borrow a venue that will accommodate your anticipated attendance and provide the requisite audio-visual capabilities to meet the speaker’s needs.
Once you’ve confirmed the basics, send a save the date no more than 10 weeks in advance. Send a real invitation with registration details at least 6 weeks prior to the event.
Create a record of the event that you can share with network members who aren’t able to make it. If the event is the first of its kind, consider inviting the press as well.

example.name: Tours & Roadshows
example.description: As part of its Together for Tomorrow initiative to strengthen partnerships among schools, families, and communities, the U.S. Department of Education visited Pittsburgh to tour Remake Learning network sites and speak with members at a listening session.

example.name: Authors & Thinkers
example.description: The Fred Rogers Center, leveraging its position as a recognized leader in early childhood education, invited author Paul Tough to speak at Saint Vincent College near Pittsburgh and read from selections of his book How Children Succeed.

example.name: National Partners
example.description: As part of its ongoing efforts to build an ecosystem for digital badges in Pittsburgh, The Sprout Fund brought Akili Lee of the Digital Youth Network to Pittsburgh to speak about DYN’s experience deploying digital badges in Chicago.

example.name: Launch Events
example.description: At the launch event for Pittsburgh City of Learning, major new initiative involving dozens of Remake Learning Network members, speakers from the MacArthur Foundation and the Badge Alliance gave remarks to reinforce how Pittsburgh connected to national efforts.

plays_group.name: Catalyze
plays_group.teaser: Empower network members to put their ideas into action by providing financial support for new initiatives and programs that directly impact children and youth, and create proof points for why learning innovation matters.

question.question_details: What are your goals for catalyzing innovation? Are you starting from scratch or are there already early-stage projects or promising new initiatives that can grow into exemplary projects?

Where would funding have the greatest impact in your community? In support of educators to deliver innovative instruction? In the creation of new and innovative learning programs? In research initiatives? In the development of new ventures and enterprises?
Where do you want to catalyze innovation? Is there a specific topic area or approach to learning that your community is focused on?
What kinds of non-financial assistance do your network members need? Are they struggling to find partners? Do they need technical support or professional development?
Who will take the overall lead in catalyzing innovation in your network?

play.name: Catalytic Grants
play.excerpt: Offer small-scale funding awards to catalyze new and innovative learning programs and projects both in-school and out-of-school so that network members have the support necessary to put their ideas into action through pilot programs, design partnerships, and product prototypes that educators and students can use to explore new ways of teaching and learning.

advice.advice_details: Write down the characteristics of the kinds of projects you seek to support, specifying the size, age, background, and geographic bounds of target audiences, the topic or content area the grants will focus on, and any requirements critical to success.

Determine the size and quantity of grants you seek to make. Projects can be catalyzed for as little as $5,000 and are most effective when they contribute to a critical mass of activity. Aim to make at least 3-5 projects in your first round.
Draft a grant application form that includes questions that help you determine if an applicant fits within your established framework.
Seat a committee of volunteers from your network who are unlikely to apply for a grant and can make objective funding decisions based on the network’s funding goals and grantmaking criteria.

Provide ongoing project assistance to funded project teams to ensure their success. Provide follow up advice to denied applicants to help them improve their application or partner with other network members.

example.name: STEAM Grants
example.description: The Allegheny Intermediate Unit distributes grants of up to $20,000 to support classroom innovation in nearly 30 Pittsburgh-area school districts.

example.name: Hive Grants
example.description: Avonworth High School used a Hive Grant from The Sprout Fund to catalyze a Connected Learning project that had students partnering with museum professionals to plan, curate, and execute an art show in their school.

example.name: Spark Grants
example.description: The Children’s Innovation Project used a Spark Grant from The Sprout Fund to formalize work they had piloted to create interdisciplinary technology programming for kindergarten students.

example.name: Funding Coalitions
example.description: Local philanthropies can also make targeted, small-scale investments in pilot projects, like the Entertainment Technology Academy at Elizabeth Forward High School which was catalyzed by a small grant from The Grable Foundation.

play.name: Project Assistance
play.excerpt: Provide value-added services to support the professional and leadership development of network members by connecting them with experienced mentors, equipping them with toolkits and guides, and partnering unincorporated groups with fiscal sponsors.

advice.advice_details: Use a simple online survey tool to find out what your network members need most. Provide them with both suggested services, as well as space to write in their own ideas.
Based on survey responses, compile a list of local support organizations and online resources you can make available to your network and outline their service offerings.
If there are local agencies interested and available to provide project assistance services to your network, reach out to them and begin a partnership. Determine a mutually beneficial arrangement.
Publish your list of available resources to your website and host a series of small info sessions to introduce network members to the new services available to them.
Meet face-to-face with network members, host a meeting or webinar, or present at a resource fair where you can introduce your menu of network supports to your target audiences.

example.name: Mentorship
example.description: The Sprout Fund matches newly funded projects with leaders of past successful projects to offer guidance and advice on common challenges facing man small-scale pilot initiatives.

example.name: Info Sessions
example.description: The Sprout Fund hosts monthly workshops for prospective grant applicants to help them understand funding criteria, partner with network members, and develop their ideas into more competitive grant applications.

example.name: Fiscal Sponsorship
example.description: Nonprofit organizations like PAEYC provide fiscal sponsorship for individuals and unincorporated groups seeking grants, like TekStart, an afterschool program for African-American youth to develop career-oriented tech skills.

example.name: Toolkits & Guides
example.description: The Digital Corps developed teaching kits to share with other afterschool programs in the network interested in using free and openly available tech learning tools to offer digital literacy programming for tweens and teens.

play.name: Research Fellows
play.excerpt: Provide research fellowships to invest in local thought leaders including researchers, scholars and practitioners who can partner with other network members to study learning innovation in practice, evaluate the effectiveness of programs, and provide informed guidance in the design or re-design of programs.

advice.advice_details: Determine how support for research fellows will contribute to the overall capacity of your network. Consider how support for graduate-level researchers would build a local brain trust, while support for more senior researchers would elevate their prominence.

Decide on a challenging question currently facing your network that researchers can begin working to answer. Consider how work toward answering the question will add value to your network members, educators, and other practitioners.

Determine the amount of money required to support both the fellow’s time and any material or technology costs to complete the work. Remake Learning research fellowships have ranged from $5,000 to $10,000.

Develop a call for research proposals that describes the main goals of the fellowship and outlines expectations for the researcher to work with network members. Share the call with local colleges and universities with research institutes in the field or research-oriented graduate programs.
Create opportunities to share the results of the fellow’s research with other network members, such as small report-out events or a high-level summary of the work with specific recommendations.

example.name: Junior Fellows
example.description: The Fred Rogers Center provides Early Career Fellowships for young professionals and graduate students interested in making a career in early childhood learning and children’s media.

example.name: Design Fellows
example.description: The University of Pittsburgh Center for Learning in Out-of-School Environments (UPCLOSE) embedded design researchers in network sites like Assemble and the Carnegie Museum of Natural History to help OST educators improve programming.

example.name: Practice Fellows
example.description: The Sprout Fund provided fellowships to graduate students and academic researchers to dive deeply into specific practices of local learning innovators, like maker education and youth media production.

example.name: Community Fellows
example.description: Professor Tom Akiva led a team of researchers from University of Pittsburgh School of Education to study how youth-serving organizations organized and supported youth advisory committees and shared recommendations with the rest of the network.

play.name: Request for Proposal
play.excerpt: Make strategic funding available through contests, competitions, or Requests for Proposal (RFP) to focus the network’s attention on issues and opportunities of critical importance, such as summer learning loss prevention, school classroom transformation, or in coordination with national campaigns like City of Learning.

advice.advice_details: Define the specific topic or challenge that is the focus of the funding opportunity, the desired impact of the supported projects, the geographic bounds of target audiences, and any requirements critical to success.
Determine the size and quantity of grants you seek to make. Local RFPs released to the Remake Learning Network have ranged from $35,000 to $50,000.

Draft a request for proposal that describes the goals of the funding opportunity, the available budget, the specific challenge or topic the applicants must focus on, and the outcomes supported projects are expected to achieve.
Seat a committee of volunteers from your network who are unlikely to apply for a grant and can make objective funding decisions based on the network’s funding goals and grantmaking criteria.

Support the strategic success of the selected projects by documenting the process and outcomes of the projects with photography, writing, and other media that will further elevate the importance of the focus area among network members.

example.name: Recipes for Remarkable Learning
example.description: The Sprout Fund issued a call for Remake Learning Network members to turn successful projects into lesson plans other educators can remix to introduce innovative learning practices in their classrooms.

example.name: City of Learning
example.description: Pittsburgh City of Learning offered small grants to organizations who responded to a request for proposals demonstrating how they would use digital badges to recognize learning in their summer programs.

example.name: Learning Through Play
example.description: To focus the Remake Learning Network’s attention on the uses of play for learning, The Sprout Fund offered grants of up to $50,000 to support new and innovative approaches to play-based learning led by regional collaboratives.

example.name: Transforming the Learning Space
example.description: The Allegheny Intermediate Unit has used its annual STEAM Grants opportunity to support innovative learning practices in Pittsburgh-area school districts to encourage school leaders to re-design classrooms, libraries, and other spaces for 21st century learning.

play.name: Incubate Ventures
play.excerpt: Establish or support existing start-up incubators where local entrepreneurs can develop emerging education technology concerns and connect with educators and researchers in the network to co-design, playtest, and evaluate new education technology products.

advice.advice_details: Partner with a business development agency, chamber of commerce, or incubator to identify ed-tech enterprises in your community or target those based elsewhere, but ready for collaboration with educators.
Based on your assessment, determine if your community possesses strengths in particular ed-tech areas such as software, hardware, game-based learning, learning management, or online learning.
Host a convening to facilitate brainstorming and exchange among educators interested in ed-tech innovation and entrepreneurs looking for input from educators.
Partner with network members interested in offering their space or programs to be used as testing ground for prototype ed-tech products.
Recruit curriculum specialists to help ed-tech enterprises develop lesson plans and curricular materials educators can use to support their application of new ed-tech products in their classrooms.
Partner with professional development agencies to develop training modules that help educators learn to use new ed-tech products emerging from incubators.

example.name: Playtesting
example.description: MAKESHOP at The Children’s Museum has been the site for ed-tech developers to test their prototype products, assisted by the museum educators and learning researchers who staff the museum exhibit.

example.name: Contests
example.description: The Forbes Funds partnered with BNY Mellon to launch UpPrize, a competitive funding opportunity offering awards of up to $1 million to support Pittsburgh entrepreneurs focusing on solving social challenges, including education innovation.

example.name: Start Up Accelerator
example.description: After developing a prototype puzzle-based programming game for kids in MAKESHOP, Digital Dream Labs went through the AlphaLab start up accelerator program to launch their first product Puzzlets.

example.name: Higher Ed Spin-Outs
example.description: CREATE Lab, a socially-oriented research and development lab within Carnegie Mellon’s Robotics Institute, has seen graduate student projects like the Finch turn into viable ed-tech businesses like BirdBrain Technologies.

play.name: National Funding Support
play.excerpt: Seek opportunities to secure funding commitments from national philanthropies, government agencies, and other stakeholders by matching network members leading in specific areas to anticipated priorities, and providing technical assistance to apply for national funding opportunities.

advice.advice_details: Do some research on current funding opportunities available from private foundations, corporate giving programs, and government agencies. If contacts are available, reach out to establish communication with program officers.

Based on your review of current funding opportunities, determine which opportunities are the best fit for your network based on your local interests, your level of network maturity, and other important factors.

After choosing an opportunity to pursue, determine who from your network will need to participate. Reach out to these partners to confirm their interest and availability to participate, and find out how they can contribute to the application.

Major funding requests can require a lot of work and back up to demonstrate your readiness for funding. Budget the appropriate amount of time to draft the application and gather any required supporting materials from partners.
During the application process, begin to sketch out how you will leverage this national funding to further develop the capacity of your network and its long-term sustainability.

example.name: MacArthur Foundation
example.description: Leveraging the network’s strength in digital media and learning initiatives, The Sprout Fund secured support from the MacArthur Foundation to support the launch of Hive Pittsburgh.

example.name: IMLS
example.description: The Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh built a reputation for rigorous and thoughtful development of maker learning practices in its MAKESHOP exhibit and secured supports from the Institute of Museum & Library Services to share their findings nationwide.

example.name: Wallace
example.description: Pittsburgh Public Schools secured support from the Wallace Foundation to support the district’s Summer Dreamers Academy, connecting the program to the national emphasis on summer enrichment.

example.name: Gates
example.description: Pittsburgh Public Schools was one of six recipients of major funding from the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation to support new methods of recruiting, developing, and evaluating educators.

plays_group.name: Communicate
plays_group.teaser: Amplify the voice of network members by documenting success, telling stories, gathering evidence, and joining the global conversation about learning innovation.

question.question_details: What are your communications goals? Are you seeking to enhance communication among network members? Are you seeking to shape public discourse? Are you seeking to increase the level of press coverage of your network?

What is your core message? What major education challenges are your network responding to? How is your network’s approach to this challenge new, innovative, and distinct? What are your best examples of effectiveness?
Who is the target of your communications? Educators? The press? Parents and families? Children and youth? What do you have to offer each and what is the best method to reach them?
What is your network’s point-of-view? Who guides the development of the network’s voice? How does your network’s voice support its mission?

What kinds of communications content would be most useful to your network? Do you need to build a media library? Do you need in-depth stories or reports? Do you need content for press outreach, social media, and blogging?
Who will take the overall lead in communicating on behalf of your network?

play.name: Blog
play.excerpt: Join the global conversation about the future of learning through a weblog where you share stories, news, and “think-pieces” with network members to keep them informed, and where network members can see their work represented within the broader context of learning innovation.

advice.advice_heading: Find a home for your blog
advice.advice_details: If you don’t already have a blog, you’ll need to create one from scratch. Choose a blogging platform, purchase a memorable domain name that represents your network, and make it look nice.
Purchase a domain and a hosting package. Find out the going rate for freelance writers in your community and determine how much work you can afford to hire.

Describe your target audience and the kinds of content your blog will serve them. Decide whether you will publish short, frequent posts about current news or longer, occasional posts that dig deeper into key topics, or a combination.
Create a calendar that guides what you plan to publish when. Work backwards from your publishing dates to set draft and final deadlines for writing assignments.
You’ll need help to review and revise blog posts, even if you plan to do most of the writing yourself. Reach out to freelance journalists, graduate students, or active bloggers in your network.
Share posts widely via your social media followers and email list subscribers. Be sure to create opportunities for people to comment and provide feedback to your blog.

example.name: Guest Posts
example.description: Network members contribute posts to the Remake Learning blog when they return from conferences, publish a new report, or discover something they want the whole network to know about.

example.name: Digest & Translate
example.description: Blog editors survey current trends and topics of discussion in the ongoing global conversation about learning and education, then relate those concepts and ideas to concrete examples happening in Pittsburgh.

example.name: Unpacking Ideas
example.description: Remake Learning runs an ongoing series of blog posts that examine specific approaches to learning that might be poorly understood, such as Blended Learning, Flipped Learning, Connected Learning, and 21st Century Learning.

example.name: Catching Up With
example.description: Remake Learning shines a rotating spotlight on individual network members so that people who have been involved for a while can reflect on how things have changed, and new members can introduce themselves and their work.

play.name: Social Media
play.excerpt: Establish a social media presence for the network that speak on behalf of the network, using shared hashtags so that network members can contribute to the conversation and rally around special opportunities, by participating in scheduled social media events, and joining the social media backchannel happening at local and national events.

advice.advice_details: Determine the purpose of your social media activities. Balance your use of social media for the purposes of directly engaging network members and for promoting the network.
If your network doesn’t already have a social media presence, create accounts on Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram in the name of your network.
Immediately follow, friend, subscribe, and like the people and organizations who form the core of your network on social media.

Identify key people and organizations in your community who are influential in your community and be sure to follow, friend, and subscribe to their social media accounts. Tag them in your messages to draw their attention to your work.

Follow specific hashtags that relate to the interests of your network, join pre-scheduled twitter chats about education and innovation, and consider organizing your own conversation around a specific event or topic using a new hashtag.
Maintain a social media calendar to keep the conversation going without having to spend every day on your social media account.

example.name: Hand Over Accounts
example.description: Remake Learning Network members are given access to the network’s twitter account @remakelearning, like when Dror Yaron of the CREATE Lab represented the network at the International Democratic Education Conference.

example.name: Join The Conversation
example.description: Remake Learning regularly participates in twitterchats like the worldwide #EdChat as well as locally focused conversations like #AfterschoolMatters hosted by network member APOST, Pittsburgh’s afterschool support agency.

example.name: Hashtag Campaigns
example.description: Remake Learning adopts hashtags that relate to its focus areas, like #PghSummerRocks to promote summer learning, #ConnectedEd to recognize teachers during connected educator month, and #TeachtheWeb to advocate for digital and web literacy.

example.name: Virtual Conference Participation
example.description: You don’t need to actually attend national conferences in order to participate. Remake Learning adds its voice to online conversations happening at events like Games for Change, SXSWedu, and others.

play.name: Conference Participation
play.excerpt: Provide stipends to send individuals or delegations of network members to relevant conferences to establish a physical presence for the network among leaders in the field and to support network members invited to present or speak at events.

advice.advice_details: Create a “shortlist” of events and conferences where you feel your network must have a presence. If possible, select multiple conferences across a range of dates throughout the calendar year.

The cost of attending a conference can vary greatly from event to event. Set a maximum budget you can afford to offer, even if it doesn’t cover all the costs. If possible, dedicate enough funding to help network members participate in at least 5-6 conferences per year.
Identify network members who can act as representatives for the whole of the network and provide them with talking points and marketing materials they can distribute and leave behind at the event.

Require network members who receive conference stipends to share what they learned with other network members in small report-out events, guest blog posts, or an interview that can be shared in your network newsletter.

example.name: Speaking Opportunities
example.description: The Sprout Fund provided conference stipends to several Remake Learning Network members who had secured speaking opportunities at the annual Digital Media & Learning Conference in June 2015.

example.name: Major National Events
example.description: Elizabeth Forward School District Assistant Superintendent Todd Keruskin utilized a conference stipend from The Sprout Fund to share the story of his district’s transformation with other educators and innovators at the annual SXSWedu event in Austin, TX.

South Fayette School District organized a Remake Learning feature event at ISTE 2015, creating opportunities for district educators and other network representatives to engage thousands of ISTE attendees in Remake Learning workshops.

example.name: Showcase Opportunities
example.description: Remake Learning Network members are supported to exhibit their innovative approaches to learning at signature showcase events like the National Maker Faire in Washington, D.C., where the Children’s Innovation Project, CREATE Lab, Digital Corps, and MAKESHOP created a strong Pittsburgh presence.

example.name: Partner with Locally Hosted National Events
example.description: When the Association of Children’s Museums hosted their annual national convening in Pittsburgh, a small amount of support for the event created an opportunity for Remake Learning Network members to be featured in a special round of ’Small Talks’ before this national audience.

play.name: Directory
play.excerpt: Create a digital directory that collects the basic information and contact details for the people, programs, and organizations that make up the network so that network members can see themselves as part of a larger whole, access a catalog of available resources and support services, and browse a calendar of upcoming events and opportunities to engage.

advice.advice_details: There are several directory tools to choose from, from WordPress blogs to wikis. Choose a system that you adapt to your needs and allow others to contribute.
Use guidelines to evaluate if new directory entries are suitable for listing. Your criteria should include a checklist of qualities that describe ideal network members.
Determine the people, projects, and organizations in your community who must be included in the first round of directory entries. These are the core participants of your network.
Reach out to your first entries and ask them to submit the required information directly to you or via a submission form process built in to the directory.
Once you’ve built out your core membership, reach out to the broader community and invite others to add themselves to the directory.

Schedule time for regular review and maintenance of the directory like revising entries for accuracy and consistency. Also consider sending regular reminders to network members to review their own entries.

example.name: People
example.description: Members of the Remake Learning Network use the people directory to share what they’ve been working on, find potential partners, and learn about members of the network they haven’t met yet.

example.name: Projects
example.description: A portfolio of project profiles provides basic details, contact info, and relevant links to help users find remarkable learning experiences for children and youth in the Greater Pittsburgh Region.

example.name: Organizations
example.description: An index of organizations that make up the Remake Learning Network, representing the range of public and private institutions, for profit companies and nonprofit agencies that add strength to the network.

example.name: Opportunities
example.description: A calendar of events, activities, and opportunities for network members helps people connect with one another face-to-face, sign up for professional development and other training sessions, and find conferences to attend.

play.name: Amplify Youth Voice
play.excerpt: Invite young people to contribute authentic stories and personal reflections on their learning experiences and other forms of participation in the network in order to create a public channel for sharing the voices of youth impacted by the network with the members themselves, as well as other audiences.

advice.advice_heading: Pick a topic to focus on
advice.advice_details: Get started by choosing a topic for youth to respond to, such as a story in the current news cycle or a topic that youth are eager to address.
Determine how you would like youth to respond, such as sharing a video on YouTube, photos on Instagram, or written stories for blog posts.
Identify programs or organizations in your community already engaging youth in storytelling or media production. Invite them to take the lead on amplifying youth voice in your network.

Issue a call for contributions and share it with youth-serving agencies in your community. Be sure to specify submission guidelines for various media and gather release forms signed by the children’s legal guardians giving you permission to share work by the youth.
Choose the best submissions and prepare them for publication, either through your own blog, or via social media using a shared hashtag to link the youth stories together.

example.name: Hear Me Project
example.description: Hear Me interviewed more than 100 Pittsburgh students about youth-police relations, then partnered with youth advocacy organization Allies for Children to share these interviews with Pittsburgh Mayor Bill Peduto as he searched for the city’s next Chief of Police.

example.name: Pgh Youth Media
example.description: SLB Radio recruits high school students interested in investigative journalism, documentary filmmaking, and radio broadcasting, then matches them with media professionals who act as mentors as the youth publish stories to their own digital news publication.

example.name: Youth Advisors
example.description: Teen programs like The Labs @ CLP build youth voice into the governance structure of their programs by seating advisory councils and decisionmaking bodies made up of the youth they serve.

example.name: Tech Warriors
example.description: Neighborhood Learning Alliance hires African American high school students and trains them to become STEM learning mentors for elementary school students, empowering the teens and giving the younger kids role models they can relate to.

play.name: Newsletter
play.excerpt: Deliver relevant and actionable content on a regular schedule, including links to relevant news stories and reports, as well as alerts about upcoming events and opportunities, so that network members can stay informed and engaged and begin to identify the network as a reliable source for information.

advice.advice_details: There are several affordable options for email marketing, including MailChimp and Constant Contact. Subscriptions typically vary based on the size of your distribution list, so set your target list size and choose a service that works for you.

Create a basic spreadsheet of the people you want to send emails to, starting with the core members of your network. Be sure to ask people for permission before sending them a mass email marketing message.
Decide what major categories of content you will include, such as major news, upcoming events, job openings, funding opportunities, current research, etc., and bookmark your sources for this content.
Create a simple, well-organized, and easy-to-understand layout for your message. Be sure to include a link to sign up for your email so that people who receive your message as a forward may sign up.
Start by sending a monthly message and adjust the frequency of your distribution cycle based on the needs of your network.

example.name: Surveys
example.description: Remake Learning uses its newsletter as a mechanism for gathering input from network members by issuing an annual survey to gauge the effectiveness of its network-building strategies.

example.name: News
example.description: To build its weekly newsletter, the Remake Learning Network subscribes to a wide range of news sources, feeds, and aggregators to surface the most relevant news stories about learning innovation both locally and nationally.

example.name: Reports
example.description: To keep network members informed and current, the Remake Learning newsletter highlights important publications like the Ed-Tech Devleoper’s Guide released by the U.S. Department of Education, or the Aspen Institute report on learning and the internet.

example.name: Event & Opportunity Alerts
example.description: Remake Learning sends a weekly message focused on a single upcoming opportunity that the network needs to know about, including major events, funding opportunities, contests for youth, and announcements of new initiatives.

play.name: Documentation & Storytelling
play.excerpt: Commission writers, photographers, videographers, and designers to produce original stories and images that capture the network in action, shine a spotlight on network success stories, and amplify the voice of individual network members.

advice.advice_details: Identify the intended audience for your documentation products and imagine the kind of story that will resonate with them and the kind of media that will reach them.
Costs vary depending on the type, quantity, and quality of the work. Videos are typically most expensive. Writing budgets often depend on the amount of original field reporting required.
Write a briefing of the key features and big ideas to be captured and an explanation of how the subject relates to your larger efforts as a network.
Hire professionals to produce the work. Search your community for photographers, videographers, and writers and reach out to those who produce work you like.
Be sure to collect signed media consent and release forms from anyone who will be included in visual media, especially minors.

Post your completed piece to your own blog and also offer the materials for syndication in other local media and allied organizations. Be sure to share links to members of your network and other targeted people via social media.
High-quality documentation, especially photos and written profiles, can be used as a rich source of evidence of the growth and impact of your network in proposals and reports.

example.name: Photography & Video & Audio
example.description: It would be impossible tell the story of a place like Elizabeth Forward School District without photo essays and video featurettes to capture the district’s transformation visually.

example.name: Profiles
example.description: To introduce new network members, Remake Learning writes brief profiles that are featured on the network’s home page so other members can get to know their peers.

example.name: Reporting & Feature Stories
example.description: Field reporting creates blanket coverage of the many small-scale innovative projects emerging from the Remake Learning Network and creates useful content for the blog, presentations, and media outreach.

example.name: Infographics
example.description: Visualizations help make complex ideas easily comprehensible, whether visualizing the impact of an individual project or creating a ready reference for practitioners like the Mindful Makers poster created by Remake Learning Network Member and University of Pittsburgh associate professor Leanne Bowler.

play.name: Press Outreach
play.excerpt: Pitch stories to local and national press contacts that highlight the exceptional work of specific network members, elevate the profile of experts and leaders within the network for quotation and comment in larger stories, and help to establish the community as a place where educators and innovators are taking concrete steps to improve learning opportunities for young people.

advice.advice_details: Define what successful press coverage means to your network, the key points you want to be covered, and set some basic goals for where and when you will secure coverage.
Identify a legitimate piece of news generated by a member of your network and begin gathering basic information like the who, what, where, and when of the story.
Craft a story that relates your news item to a topic or event that will likely generate coverage in your local media market.
This can be as simple as press release announcing a new initiative or a media advisory inviting coverage of an event, or as in-depth as a background briefing about your network.
Get to know the reporters and editors working in your community. Look for contacts who are already writing about education, youth and family issues, and innovation.
Send personal messages to your press list targets with your background materials attached. Follow up with a phone call if you don’t hear back within a day.

example.name: Funding Announcements
example.description: Money grabs people’s attention. Remake Learning has consistently drawn media coverage when announcing STEAM Grants to regional school districts, and when receiving major investments from national funders like the MacArthur Foundation.

example.name: Event Hooks
example.description: Public events, especially those that directly engage children and youth in creative, hands-on, and visually rich activities like the Pittsburgh Maker Party, are great for attracting local TV stations and newspapers.

example.name: Launching New Campaign
example.description: News has to be new. When Pittsburgh City of Learning launched in 2014 with the promise of engaging thousands of youth in innovative summer programming, local media recognized the news value of the initiative.

example.name: Timing the News Cycle
example.description: Rather than pitching stories that lead with complex ideas about the future of learning, identify topics already in the local news cycle and show your press contacts how your network can move the needle on those issues.

example.name: Human Interest
example.description: There’s nothing like a personal story to demonstrate the impact of your work, like Pittsburgh teenager Caroline Combemale who went from attending digital learning workshops at The Labs @ CLP to interning at Assemble, to leading her own peer-to-peer digital learning program.

play.name: Publications
play.excerpt: Publish documents that report on network activities and accomplishments and capture and share the best of the network’s learnings that can act as resource guides for others seeking to implement similar programs and strategies.

advice.advice_details: Choose the kind of document you will produce, such as a document that summarizes the network, a resource guide that contains practicable guidance for educators in your network, or a promotional piece that highlights your network’s success stories.
Recruit an expert from your network to draft original content, an editor to shape and polish written content, and a designer to design an attractive and functional product.

Estimate the budget of your publication based on the cost of writing, editing, designing, printing, and distributing your publication. Keep in mind that per-unit printing costs can decrease dramatically as the quantity of copies increases.
Choose a date when you will need to have publications in-hand and work back from there, factoring several weeks for the printing, designing, editing, and writing phases of the work.

As the final publication reaches completion, begin alerting your network members, as well as external audiences and press targets, to generate anticipation for the publication. Identify members of your network who can help distribute a portion of publications.

example.name: State of the Network Report
example.description: Remake Learning issues an annual ’State of the Network Report’ that records the growth and evolution of the network, recognizes major developments and accomplishments, and summarizes the results of the annual network survey.

example.name: University Press
example.description: CREATE Lab Director Dr. Illah Nourbakhsh published Robot Futures through MIT Press, exploring how new technologies will shape the future of life and work, and the opportunities communities have to shape this next evolution of society for the best.

example.name: Teaching Kits
example.description: The Digital Corps publishes Teaching Kits developed with contributions from a variety of network members to share locally-developed programming as a Remake Learning contribution to the international movement to #teachtheweb.

example.name: Applied Research Reports
example.description: University of Pittsburgh researcher Tom Akiva studied how out-of-school learning programs built youth leadership opportunities into their programs and shared recommendations for designing and managing youth advisory councils in a Remake Learning report.

play.name: From Local to National
play.excerpt: Share examples of network success with influential audiences by inviting peers, policymakers, researchers, and funders to visit and tour the network and by seeking opportunities to showcase network success at national events focusing on learning innovation.

advice.advice_details: Create a list of foundations, think tanks, publications, and influential people who need to know about your network. Gather their contact information and make notes of their particular interest.
Identify a "shortlist" of exemplary places, projects, and organizations that best represent your network and relate to the interests of your national targets.

Invite people from your list of national targets to visit your community and see how you are remaking learning. Be sure to include some high-quality documentation to give them a preview of what they’ll see when they visit.

Make a list of people from your network who can be recognized as experts in their field and equip them with talking points and background materials about the network to share during their next interview.

example.name: Innovation Tours
example.description: Elizabeth Forward School District hosts regular monthly tours of its school, attracting visitors from more than 100 school districts throughout the country to see how district leaders, educators, facility staff, and students are all contributing to a transformed school environment.

example.name: User Communities
example.description: BirdBrain Technologies maintains online forums to build virtual communities of teachers across the country as a way to grow its user and customer base organically, and also serve up examples of how Remake Learning Network members are using their education technology products.

example.name: Expert Consultation
example.description: When the Obama Administration wanted to host the first ever White House Maker Faire, The Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh shared the lessons learned they’ve learned in MAKESHOP and were recognized for their leadership in maker education.

example.name: For Attribution
example.description: Remake Learning Network members with expertise in particular fields are served up to writers and reporters seeking quotes from authoritative sources, such as CREATE Lab director Dr. Illah Nourbakhsh in robotics or Dr. Junlei Li of the Fred Rogers Center in early childhood learning.

plays_group.name: Coordinate
plays_group.teaser: Establish a structure for the network that enables individual members to do what they do best, while also collaborating across sectors and sharing resources effectively.

question.question_details: How will network coordination contribute to building your network’s capacity? How will network members leverage cooperation to support their own goals?

What barriers may be preventing coordination from happening naturally? Is there a gap in communication that you can help to close? Are there legal, procedural, or financial obstacles the network can smooth out?
How will greater coordination help your network develop and achieve long-term outcomes for your network, and be more effective operating strategic initiatives?

How will you coordinate your network’s activities with larger, national or international efforts? Will you seek partnerships that bring specific resources or talents to your region? Will you seek to join national or international networks that share your local goals?
Who in your network can take the lead in coordinating network members?

play.name: Program Cooperation
play.excerpt: Connect peer organizations offering complementary programming to help initiate collaboration and exchange among network member organizations, creating opportunities for traveling programs to deploy activities in established learning spaces like libraries and community centers as a means of enhancing the reach and effectiveness of learning programs while also developing staff capacity and responsiveness to target audiences.

advice.advice_details: Gather information from network members to learn about current programmatic offerings and create an inventory of programs that may be suitable for deployment in sites throughout your network.

Inquire with schools and youth-serving organizations to learn about their interest in hosting outside programming, understand their needs, and determine ways to supplement their capacities through matches with program providers.
Use convening and catalyzing strategies to jumpstart cooperation among network members and remove any obstacles that might prevent cooperation to naturally arise.

Work with program providers to prepare their activities for off-site deployment by organizing traveling materials kits, developing flexible lesson plans to be delivered in a variety of settings and timeframes, and leave behind materials for ongoing activities.
As your network develops a robust inventory of programmatic offerings and youth-serving host sites, develop a platform for network members to connect with each other, such as a shared calendar.

example.name: Programming Hubs
example.description: The Labs @ CLP expands the diversity of programs it offers, and becomes even more a hub for youth, by partnering with outside organizations who deliver programming ranging from video production to installation art.

example.name: Digital Corps
example.description: The Digital Corps provides cash-strapped afterschool sites in Pittsburgh with an easy and affordable way to expand their programmatic offerings, and build their own staff capacity to deliver digital literacy programming.

example.name: School Enrichment
example.description: Assemble partners with school districts to provide ongoing STEAM learning enrichment programming during the school day, supplementing student’s in-school experience and building bridges to extended-day programming after school.

example.name: Mobile MAKESHOP
example.description: The Children’s Museum partnered with community centers and libraries to deliver mobile maker programs and expand access to hands-on maker learning experiences for youth who may not have the opportunity to visit the museum’s MAKESHOP exhibit.

play.name: National to Local
play.excerpt: Reach out to organizations leading change on the national level and seek opportunities to partner with them to implement localized programming that helps connect your community with the global movement to remake learning.

advice.advice_details: Survey the landscape of national education innovation movements, including research initiatives, communities of practice, academic networks, publications, and media properties.

Find network member organizations who can take responsibility for the local adaptation and implementation of national initiatives. Focus on matching the assets and resources network members possess with the local needs of national initiatives.
Invite representatives to visit your community and see how you are remaking learning. Demonstrate your community’s readiness to implement local programming based on a national model.

While only a small number of network members may have the capacity to take on a national initiative, be sure to build in mechanisms for sharing knowledge gained with your broader network through events, workshops, or publications.
Whenever possible, offer up local innovations to your new national partners that they can use as proof points or models for how their work is being implemented in communities.
Securing national support immediately expands your circle of colleagues and professional contacts. Consider how these new connections will help build capacity in other areas of your network.

example.name: City of Learning
example.description: Pittsburgh joined a vanguard of cities to launch the national Cities of Learning campaign in 2014, joining Chicago, Dallas, and others in creating a citywide ecosystem for deploying digital badges to recognize learning.

example.name: Maker Party
example.description: The Sprout Fund catalyzed Pittsburgh’s participation in the Mozilla’s annual global Maker Party campaign by coordinating small-scale hands-on digital learning events in neighborhoods throughout Pittsburgh.

example.name: Learning Labs
example.description: After piloting a digital learning space for teens, The Labs @ CLP joined the national Learning Labs cohort to access additional resources and connect with other innovative libraries across the U.S.

example.name: CommonSense Media
example.description: Through the support of the Grable Foundation, CommonSense Media embedded a staff member in the Pittsburgh region to work directly with school teachers and administrators, as well as network members more generally, to make better learning media choices.

play.name: Network Strategy
play.excerpt: Set an agenda for the network and establish a shared vision, common values, and long term goals by forming advisory groups of key stakeholders, surveying network members, and seating leadership councils representing influential members of the community.

advice.advice_heading: Define the need for a strategy
advice.advice_details: Describe the need for a network strategy and the anticipated benefits of establishing a shared strategy. Create a rationale so that network members understand the need and invest in the strategy development process.
Research strategic planning methods and models to develop your familiarity with the process. Give particular attention to models for open innovation and collaborative networks.
Create a survey tool, interview template, or collaborative workspace where network members can contribute to the development of the strategy.
Invite network members to gather together face-to-face or online to reflect on the strategy in development, share their thoughts, and generate ideas for putting the strategy into practice.

Once the strategy document is developed to a suitable state, post it permanently in an easily accessible web space and distribute copies to key network members. Consider writing a blog post that can act as an executive summary or guide to understanding the strategy.

Your network strategy will be a living document. Create a process for checking in on a regular basis to evaluate your network’s progress, revise any aspects of the strategy, and report-out to the network.

example.name: Periodic Strategy Review
example.description: Remake Learning Network intermediary organizations like The Sprout Fund, the Allegheny Intermediate Unit, and Carnegie Mellon University meet quarterly to share updates and coordinate future strategic initiatives.

example.name: Vision Formation Process
example.description: In 2011, The Sprout Fund issued surveys, conducted workshops, and met one-on-one with key network members to formulate a shared vision, common values, and desired outcomes for the Remake Learning Network.

example.name: Remake Learning Council
example.description: In 2014, a blue-ribbon committee of regional leaders representing the education, business, philanthropic, and government sectors came together to form the Remake Learning Council and demonstrate long-term support for the network.

example.name: Learning Competencies Working Groups
example.description: More than 100 educators, experts, and network members worked together to develop a shared set of learning competencies that can provide a rigorous underpinning for the development of digital badges for learning.

play.name: Network Research
play.excerpt: Partner with researchers to establish mechanisms for understanding and evaluating the impact of the network on its members and on the children, youth, and families it serves in order to gather evidence and data to make a stronger case for support.

advice.advice_details: Determine the specific question you are seeking to answer about your network and its impact on your target audiences.

Choose a measurable factor so that you can quantify the network’s impact. Consider using common metrics for measuring learning outcomes and student engagement such as high school graduation rates and dropout rates.

Partner with a research institution or government agency that is already engaged in gathering and analyzing data about students in your region. Work with your partner to establish a baseline measurement.

Task network members with collecting information about the students involved in their programs. Provide network members with a standard data-gathering instrument such as an entry/exit questionnaire, survey, or scorecard.
Work with your data partner to determine if any correlation or causation exists between your network’s activities and the changes you see in the metrics.
Create opportunities to share the results of the fellow’s research with other network members, such as small report-out events or a high-level summary of the work with specific recommendations.

example.name: Meta-Analysis
example.description: The Learning Media and Design Center at CMU is conducting a national review of practice-based learning research to establish a common measurement strategy for evaluating the impact of the Remake Learning Network as a whole.

example.name: Project Outcomes
example.description: Remake Learning Network members report on the successes and challenges they face as they implement grant-supported learning innovation projects, contributing to the network’s collective capacity to deliver innovative programming.

example.name: Graduate Student Contributions
example.description: Student teams from Carnegie Mellon’s Entertainment Technology Center conduct research and development projects to study the impact of transformational technology on learning outcomes both in school and out-of-school.

example.name: National Research Funding
example.description: The Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh secured support from the Institute of Museum & Library Services to study family learning in the museum’s MAKESHOP exhibit and develop design principles to guide others in developing similar programs.

plays_group.name: Champion
plays_group.teaser: Lift up the best of the network and celebrate the educators, innovators, and young people who contribute to and benefit from network activities.

question.question_details: What is the value of increasing exposure of your network’s brand? Are you seeking to engage the public in your network? Are you seeking to raise funds?

Who are you seeking to celebrate or attract to the network? Current network members? Young people? Tech companies? Funders? Government leaders? What do you have to offer each of your target audiences?
What do you want the network to look and feel like to your target audiences? What kinds of events, activities, and content support and reinforce this impression?
Once you’ve got your audience’s attention, what do you want them to do? Visit a website? Attend an event? Apply for a grant? Make choices differently?
Who will take the overall lead in championing your network?

play.name: Showcase
play.excerpt: Organize interactive exhibits that showcase exemplary network projects and programs at public events like arts fairs, summer fests, holiday events, and other gatherings that attract large numbers of children, youth, and families so that more people can have personal, hands-on experiences with learning innovation.

advice.advice_details: Identify a small group of network members who can deliver engaging face-to-face activities for learners. Aim for diversity of participants and activity types. It helps if you pay them a small daily stipend for their time.

Determine the amount of space you will be provided at the event, as well as your technical resources like electricity and internet, and sketch out how you will layout the space, keeping in mind how people will flow through it.
Create signage, banners, and take-aways that feature your network’s brand and display them prominently around the space. Provide all exhibitors with a simple set of talking points.
Issue a media advisory (or add yourself to one the event organizers are sending out) that describe your network’s presence and highlight the visual appeal for press photographers or local TV news.
Take photos of your exhibit and share them via social media or on your blog to show how your network is changing the look and feel of learning in your community.

example.name: Existing Community Festivals
example.description: In Pittsburgh, thousands of people engage with Remake Learning showcases at well-known and highly attended large scale free events like the International Children’s Festival, the Three Rivers Arts Festival, and the First Night New Year’s Eve festival.

example.name: Tap Network Ambassadors
example.description: Assemble coordinates the Remake Learning Troupe, a cadre of artists, educators, mentors, and performers who create custom showcase exhibits to represent the network at a range of community events.

example.name: Pop-up Activities
example.description: The Digital Corps partners with neighborhood organizations to host small-scale pop-up learning events throughout the city, expanding awareness and access to Remake Learning programming.

example.name: New Major Events
example.description: The Children’s Museum of Pittsburgh hosted the Pittsburgh Mini-Maker Faire for several years to raise awareness of and engagement with maker learning among the broader community.

play.name: Event Sponsorship
play.excerpt: Provide financial support and lend the network’s name to events, workshops, camps, conferences, and professional development sessions that introduce educators and others to new and innovative teaching and learning practices.

advice.advice_details: Write down the characteristics of the kinds of projects you seek to support, specifying the size, age, background, and geographic bounds of target audiences, the topic or content area the grants will focus on, and any requirements critical to success.
Determine the size and quantity of sponsorships you can afford offer. For comparison, Remake Learning event sponsorships are available up to $5,000 and the average size is $1,000.
Develop a comprehensive list of events offered by network members in your community, as well as events where you believe a network presence would be valuable.

Decide whether you will offer an ongoing open call for sponsorship requests, or make sponsorships by invitation only. Either way, request sponsorship options from applicants that outline commitment levels and corresponding sponsor recognition benefits.

Use your social media and, when appropriate, press outreach strategies to help drive attendance to sponsored events. When possible, send network representatives to speak and distribute network promotional materials.

example.name: Events for Educators
example.description: Educators in Pittsburgh used sponsorship support from Remake Learning to launch a local Ed Camp ’unconference’ series for teachers and out-of-school educators to network with one another around common interests.

example.name: Events for Children & Families
example.description: Hive Pittsburgh sponsored Youth Invasion, an annual teen event hosted by The Andy Warhol Museum, as a strategy to engage hundreds of local youth in the launch of Hive programming.

example.name: Engaging with the Community
example.description: The Sprout Fund offers $500 sponsorships to create pop-up events hosted by community organizations in neighborhoods where Remake Learning programming has not yet reached critical mass.

example.name: Creating Space for the Network
example.description: By sponsoring the Flipped Learning Conference in 2014, Remake Learning was able to secure dedicated space and time to host a network showcase for more than 200 educators visiting Pittsburgh from around the country.

play.name: Awards
play.excerpt: Recognize excellence among network members and celebrate the work of young people involved in network programs by hosting new or partnering with established events where awards and prizes can be given to elevate the best of the network and inspire others to achieve similar results.

advice.advice_details: Survey local and national contests and awards opportunities to nominate network members for.
If you’re launching your own awards ceremony, partner with an established and well-respected organization in your network to add value to the awards opportunity.
Make sure that your award is different and unique among existing local offerings. Consider adapting a national model to the local community.

Publicize the opportunity through your network communications channels and through network partners who communicate directly with eligible nominees. Provide clear instructions for how award seekers can apply or be nominated.
Choose to use a jury or public voting approach. Whichever approach you decide, make sure nominees and the public understand the award criteria.
Partner with an existing awards event or host your own to honor nominees and winners publicly. Be sure to document the event and share the good news via the network blog and social media outlets.
Issue a media advisory (or add yourself to the event organizers are sending out) that promotes the new awards and highlights the winners.

example.name: Tech & Innovation
example.description: At its annual CREate Festival celebrating technological creativity in a variety of fields and industries, The Pittsburgh Technology Council devotes a track of awards to local education innovators, putting Remake Learning Network members on par with emerging entrepreneurs.

example.name: Youth Creativity
example.description: The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh hosts the Labsy Awars, an annual ceremony recognizing original creations, inventions, and works of art by teenagers participating programming at the Labs @ CLP.

example.name: Coordinated Nominations
example.description: The Sprout Fund coordinated nominations of Remake Learning Network members to the Digital Innovation in Learning Awards, a national call for innovative educators hosted by edSurge and Digital Promise, securing two awards for network members in 2014.

example.name: Press Spotlight
